source_text: Et haec quidem, velut de publica forma humanae conditionis in suffragium carni procuraverim. Videamus nunc de propria etiam christiani nominis forma, quanta huic substantiae, frivolae ac sordidae, apud Deum praerogativa sit: et si sufficeret illi, quod nulla omnino anima salutem possit adipisci, nisi dum est in carne crediderit: adeo caro salutis est cardo. Denique cum anima Deo allegitur, ipsa est quae efficit ut anima allegi possit. Scilicet caro abluitur, ut anima emaculetur; caro ungitur, ut anima consecretur; caro signatur, ut et anima muniatur; caro manus impositione adumbratur, ut et anima spiritu illuminetur; caro corpore et sanguine Christi vescitur, ut et anima Deo saginetur. Non possunt ergo separari in mercede, quas opera conjungit. Nam et sacrificia Deo grata, conflictationes dico animae, jejunia, et seras et aridas escas, et appendices hujus officii sordes, caro de proprio suo incommodo instaurat. Virginitas quoque et viduitas, et modesta in occulto matrimonii dissimulatio, et una notitia ejus, de bonis carnis Deo adolentur. Age jam, quid de ea sentis, cum pro nominis fide in medium extracta, et odio publico exposita, decertat; cum in carceribus maceratur, teterrimo lucis exilio, penuria mundi, squalore, paedore, contumelia victus; ne somno quidem libera, quippe ipsis etiam cubilibus vincta ipsisque stramentis lancinata; cum jam et in luce omni tormentorum machinatione laniatur; cum denique suppliciis erogatur, enisa reddere Christo vicem, moriendo pro ipso, et quidem per eamdem crucem saepe, nedum per atrociora quoque ingenia poenarum? Nec illa beatissima et gloriosissima, quae potest apud Christum Dominum parere debito tanto, ut hoc solum debeat ei quod ei debere desierit; hoc magis vincta, quod absoluta.
pass_a_gloss: And indeed, as if from the public form of the human condition, I have procured a vote for the flesh. Let us see now also from the proper form of the Christian name, how great a privilege this substance, frivolous and sordid, has with God: and if it were enough for it, that no soul at all can attain salvation, unless while it is in the flesh it has believed: so much so that the flesh is the hinge of salvation. Finally, when the soul is chosen by God, it is the flesh which brings it about that the soul can be chosen. Certainly the flesh is washed, so that the soul may be cleansed; the flesh is anointed, so that the soul may be consecrated; the flesh is signed, so that the soul also may be fortified; the flesh is overshadowed by the imposition of hands, so that the soul also may be illuminated by the Spirit; the flesh feeds on the body and blood of Christ, so that the soul also may be nourished by God. Therefore, they cannot be separated in reward, whom their works join together. For also the sacrifices pleasing to God, I say the struggles of the soul, fasts, and dry and barren foods, and the filthy appendages of this duty, the flesh restores at its own expense. Virginity also and widowhood, and modest concealment of marriage, and the single knowledge of it, are offered to God from the goods of the flesh. Come now, what do you think about it, when, drawn out into the midst for the faith of the name, and exposed to public hatred, it contends; when it is worn away in prisons, in the most terrible exile of light, in want of the world, in squalor, in stench, in contempt of food; not even free from sleep, indeed bound even by the very beds and torn by the very straw; when already it is torn apart by every device of torments in the light; when finally it is expended in punishments, having been forced to repay Christ in kind, dying on behalf of him, and indeed often through the same cross, not to mention through even more atrocious kinds of punishments? Nor is it less blessed and glorious, which can be owing to Christ the Lord such a great debt, that it owes it to him that it has ceased to owe it to him; it is more bound, because it is absolved.

pass_b_english: I have, as it were, won a verdict for the flesh from the common lot of the human condition. Now let us examine the privilege this frivolous, sordid substance enjoys with God on the strength of the Christian name alone—and consider whether it would be enough that no soul can attain salvation unless it has believed while still in the flesh, making the flesh the very hinge of salvation. When God chooses a soul, it is the flesh that makes that choice possible: the flesh is washed so the soul may be cleansed; the flesh is anointed so the soul may be consecrated; the flesh is signed so the soul may be fortified; the flesh is overshadowed by the laying on of hands so the soul may be illuminated by the Spirit; the flesh feeds on the body and blood of Christ so the soul may be nourished by God. They cannot be divided in reward when their works bind them together. The sacrifices that please God—the soul's struggles, fasts, dry and meager fare, the filthy by-products of this discipline—the flesh restores at its own expense. Virginity and widowhood, the modest concealment of marriage, even the mere knowledge of it—these are offered to God from the goods of the flesh. So tell me: what do you make of it when the flesh is dragged into the arena for the faith, exposed to public hatred, and fights? When it wastes away in prisons, in the most terrible exile from light, in destitution, squalor, stench, and contempt for food—not even sleep is free, bound by the very pallets and torn by the very straw? When it is ripped apart in broad daylight by every engine of torture? When it is finally spent in punishments, forced to repay Christ in kind by dying for him, often on the very same cross, to say nothing of even more atrocious punishments? Nor is it less blessed and glorious: it can owe Christ the Lord so great a debt that it owes him only because it has ceased to owe him; it is more bound, because it is absolved.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding the relationship between the flesh and the soul. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Latin source. The nuances of 'suffragium' (vote/verdict), 'cardo' (hinge), and the paradoxical concluding sentence regarding debt and absolution are handled correctly in both versions.

The Latin text is correctly identified as 'On the Resurrection of the Flesh VIII' from the specified edition. The translation accurately reflects the source text, preserving all key arguments, negations, agency, modality, and doctrine. Scripture citations are not present in the source, so no issues arise in that area. The title 'Flesh's Role in Salvation' appropriately names the thought of the passage.
